Calling withdrawReward should never revert for any recipient (i.e., withdrawReward always succeeds).
Calling withdrawReward with any recipient that currently has a nonzero rewardsForA[...] should not revert (i.e., withdrawReward succeeds whenever the recorded reward amount is > 0).

Calling withdrawReward(address) on C should not revert when the contract's recorded reward for that recipient is equal to the exact Ether value sent out by C (i.e., the recipient's owed reward matches the value transfer amount).
Calling withdrawReward(recip) should not revert when the contract's balance is at least the recorded reward for that recipient.

For any recipient, after calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus(recipient) the reference contract always leaves rewardsForA[recipient] == 0 (i.e. no residual reward), while the mutant may leave it non-zero (1) for some inputs when the low-level call succeeds — the test detects that difference by observing the public getter for rewardsForA.

For any recipient, after calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus(recipient) the reference contract always leaves rewardsForA[recipient] == 0, while the mutant that sets rewardsForA[recipient] = 1 before the external call will leave rewardsForA[recipient] == 1 for some recipients (when the external call succeeds), breaking the rule.

For any recipient, after calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus(recipient) the reference contract always leaves address(c).balance decreased by the bonus amount and rewardsForA[recipient] == 0, while the mutant that sets rewardsForA[recipient]=1 before the external call can leave the contract with 1 wei still recorded for that recipient (i.e. rewardsForA[recipient] != 0) when the external call succeeds — the test checks the general rule that rewardsForA[recipient] == 0 by observing the public getter and fails for the mutant for some fuzzed recipient/amount when an adversarial payable callee accepts the funds.

For any recipient, after calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus(recipient) on the correct contract, rewardsForA[recipient] is reset to 0 (no leftover recorded reward); the mutant that sets rewardsForA[recipient]=1 before the external call can leave rewardsForA[recipient]==1 for some recipients (when the external call succeeds), breaking this invariant.

For any recipient and any reward amount, calling withdrawReward atomically zeroes the stored reward on success in the reference; the mutant that zeros after the external call can leave the stored reward non-zero when the external call reverts, breaking the rule.

For any recipient and any stored reward, a successful call to withdrawReward always leaves rewardsForA[recipient] == 0 in the reference; the mutant that zeros after the external call can leave rewardsForA non-zero when the recipient call reverts, so a failing callee distinguishes them.

For any recipient and any stored reward amount, a successful or reverted external call behavior to withdrawReward does not leave rewardsForA[recipient] non-zero after the call in the reference (it always zeroes before the external call), but the mutant that zeroes after the external call can leave rewardsForA[recipient] non-zero when the callee reverts, so there exists a callee that reverts which makes the mutant differ from the reference.

For any recipient and any stored reward amount, a successful call to withdrawReward always leaves rewardsForA[recipient] == 0 in the correct contract; the mutant that zeroes storage after the external call can leave rewardsForA[recipient] non-zero when the recipient reverts, so a reverting callee distinguishes them.

For any recipient and any reward amount, a successful or reverted external call to withdrawReward on the reference contract always results in rewardsForA[recipient] being cleared (0) after the call completes; the mutant that zeroes storage after the external call can leave rewardsForA[recipient] non-zero when the recipient call reverts, so a reverting callee breaks this rule.

After any successful call to withdrawReward(recipient) the contract remains unlocked in the reference (so a second withdrawReward call does not revert), while the mutant leaves the contract locked and thus a subsequent withdrawReward call reverts; the test asserts that two sequential withdrawReward calls by the same recipient both succeed on the reference but the mutant can make the second fail.

After a successful withdrawReward(recipient) call that transfers out Ether, the reference contract remains unlocked so a subsequent withdrawReward(recipient) call (even if the callee's low-level call fails) will reflect that the second call does not permanently lock the contract state — i.e., the reference does not leave the contract permanently locked after a withdraw, whereas the mutant that never resets _locked can cause subsequent withdraw attempts to permanently revert; the test uses a callee that reverts on receiving Ether to trigger the observable difference.

property_summary: Calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus on a fresh recipient never reverts in the original but can revert in the mutant; therefore for any recipient who hasn't yet claimed the bonus, the call succeeds (reverted == false).
For any recipient address, calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus(recipient) should not revert when the recipient has not yet claimed the bonus.
For a recipient who has not already claimed the bonus, calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus(recipient) should not revert (i.e., reverted == false).
For a recipient that hasn't claimed the bonus, calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus(recipient) should not revert.

For every call to getFirstWithdrawalBonus(recipient) on the correct contract, the recipient's claimedBonus becomes true only after a successful external withdrawal (so a reentrant attacker cannot both receive funds and re-enter to get another bonus); the mutant that sets claimedBonus before withdrawing allows a reentrant recipient to observe/obtain the bonus twice, violating this invariant for some attacker addresses.

For any recipient, after calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus(recipient) on the correct contract, the recipient cannot re-enter during its withdrawal to obtain the bonus twice (i.e., getFirstWithdrawalBonus can be executed at most once successfully by a reentrant malicious recipient); the mutant that marks claimedBonus before withdraw allows a reentrant recipient to reenter and receive the bonus twice, violating this invariant.

For any recipient, calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus(recipient) on the correct contract always results in the contract transferring exactly one 100-unit bonus (so the recipient cannot reenter and receive the bonus twice); the mutant that sets claimedBonus before withdraw allows a reentrant recipient to reenter during the withdrawal and obtain the bonus twice, violating this rule.

For every recipient address and attacker contract, calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus(recipient) on the correct contract never succeeds if the recipient reenters and the reentrant call would attempt to call getFirstWithdrawalBonus again during the external withdrawal (the reference's nonReentrant/ordering prevents double-awarding), whereas the mutant that sets claimedBonus before withdrawing allows a reentrant recipient to successfully cause a second award and thus changes observable state — so the property: any call to getFirstWithdrawalBonus(recipient) that reenters during the external call must revert (i.e., the overall external invocation cannot complete successfully when the callee reenters).

For any recipient contract that reverts when receiving funds, calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus(recipient) on the correct contract C always completes successfully (because the withdrawal must revert and thus bonus is not marked claimed nor funds lost), whereas the mutant that marks claimedBonus before withdraw will still mark the bonus claimed despite the external call reverting, causing claimedBonus[recipient] to be true after a failing withdrawal.

After calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus once for recipient, recipient's balance increases by exactly the bonus amount when the contract sends funds (i.e., getFirstWithdrawalBonus causes an immediate withdrawal).

Calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus reverts whenever the contract would try to send Ether to a recipient with zero withdrawal amount available (i.e., the call reverts on this input), so the invariant is that for all inputs the observed reverted flag must equal whether the recipient had no withdrawable reward at time of call.
The call to getFirstWithdrawalBonus must revert (i.e., reverted == true).
Calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus(recipient) should revert.
The call to getFirstWithdrawalBonus(recipient) must revert.

For any recipient, immediately after calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus(recipient) the contract's rewardsForA[recipient] is zero because the reference withdraws the bonus atomically, whereas the mutant that omits the withdraw leaves rewardsForA[recipient] increased (non-zero) for some inputs.

For any recipient, after calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus(recipient) on the correct contract C, the contract will attempt to send the bonus out so that address(c).balance does not increase due to that call (the bonus is withdrawn), whereas the mutant that omits the withdraw will retain the bonus in contract balance for some recipient addresses (so address(c).balance increases).

For every recipient address, calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus(recipient) on the correct contract either succeeds and leaves rewardsForA[recipient] == 0 (because the contract immediately withdraws the bonus), or reverts; the mutant that omits the withdraw will always leave rewardsForA[recipient] increased (non-zero) for some recipient, so there exist inputs where the correct contract results in rewardsForA[recipient] == 0 while the mutant leaves it > 0.

For any recipient whose fallback reverts, C's getFirstWithdrawalBonus will revert (because withdrawReward tries to send and require(success)), while the mutant that removed the withdraw will NOT revert and will mark claimedBonus true — so there exist recipients (reverting contracts) for which reference reverts but mutant succeeds.

After calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus and then withdrawReward for the same recipient, the recipient receives at least as much Ether as the contract's balance decreased (i.e., address(c).balance decreases by the withdrawn amount) — equivalent to: address(c).balance before >= after, and the withdrawn amount equals the prior reward (so recipient balance increases by that reward).

property_summary: getFirstWithdrawalBonus never reverts when called for an address that has not yet claimed a bonus
For any recipient who has not yet claimed a bonus, calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus should not revert (i.e., it must succeed).

If the caller provides a nonzero existing reward balance for the recipient, getFirstWithdrawalBonus will not revert (i.e., it succeeds) on the original contract but can revert in the mutant that overwrites instead of increments.

If the recipient already has a nonzero reward, calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus should succeed (not revert) because the contract increments the reward then withdraws, but the mutant that overwrites may revert when withdraw attempts to send more than available.

For any recipient, calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus(recipient) always results in that recipient having their rewardsForA balance equal to 0 afterwards (because the function immediately withdraws the reward); the mutant that assigns rewardsForA[recipient]=100 instead of incrementing can cause the final stored reward to differ and thus violate that property for some inputs.

For any recipient and any prior rewards value, calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus(recipient) on the correct contract always leaves the stored rewardsForA[recipient] equal to 0 (because the function adds 100 then immediately withdraws and sets it to 0), whereas the mutant that assigns rewardsForA[recipient] = 100 can leave a nonzero stored reward for some inputs (when the external call fails), thus violating this property.

For any recipient and any prior state, calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus(recipient) on the correct contract never leaves a nonzero rewardsForA[recipient] after the call completes (the contract always ends with zero owed), while the mutant that assigns rewardsForA[recipient] = 100 can leave a nonzero stored reward when the low-level transfer to recipient fails.

For every recipient and any prior rewardsForA value, if the recipient's fallback ALWAYS reverts (making the low-level call in withdrawReward fail), then the reference contract preserves the previous rewardsForA[recipient] value after getFirstWithdrawalBonus (because it added 100 then the failed withdraw leaves rewardsForA unchanged), whereas the mutant that assigns rewardsForA[recipient] = 100 will overwrite the prior balance and thus change rewardsForA[recipient] for some inputs (i.e., the mutant can reduce or change the stored reward when the external call fails).

For any recipient and any prior rewardsForA value, calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus(recipient) on the reference C always restores rewardsForA[recipient] to its previous value if the external call to recipient reverts, while the mutant that assigns rewardsForA[recipient] = 100 can overwrite and thus change the stored rewardsForA when the recipient's receive/fallback reverts.

Calling getFirstWithdrawalBonus once for a recipient never leaves rewardsForA[recipient] nonzero after the call (recipient receives withdrawal), i.e., address(c).balance decreases by at least the added bonus amount.
